The conditions a ≠ b ≠ c together with α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90° define the triclinic system —
the least symmetric of the seven, where all three edges and all three angles differ.
Match each salt to its system:
K₂Cr₂O₇ — triclinic ✓
NaNO₃ — rhombohedral (a = b = c, α = β = γ ≠ 90°)
KNO₃ — orthorhombic (a ≠ b ≠ c, α = β = γ = 90°)
K₂SO₄ — orthorhombic
Only the triclinic one has no right angle anywhere and no two edges equal.
∴ K₂Cr₂O₇.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|19||0|0:
Check each statement against the definitions.
(A) False — Frenkel defect needs a *large* difference in ion sizes. A small cation can squeeze
into an interstitial site; that is why ZnS and AgBr show it and NaCl does not.
(C) False — an F-centre is an *electron* trapped in an anion vacancy, not a proton. The trapped
electron absorbs visible light, which is why the crystal becomes coloured.
(D) False — Schottky defect removes equal numbers of cations and anions from the lattice, so
the mass falls while the volume does not: the density decreases.
(B) True — in a Frenkel defect an ion leaves its lattice site and lodges in an interstitial site.
It is dislocated rather than lost, so the defect is a dislocation defect and the density is unchanged.
∴ Frenkel defect is a dislocation defect.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|20||0|0:
Count the share of each atom that belongs to one unit cell.
A at the corners: a corner is shared by 8 cells, so each contributes ⅛.
B at the face centres: a face is shared by 2 cells, so each contributes ½.
With all corners occupied: A = 8 × ⅛ = 1 and B = 6 × ½ = 3, giving AB₃.
Now remove one corner A, leaving 7 corners:
A = 7 × ⅛ = ⅞
B = 6 × ½ = 3 (unchanged)
Ratio A : B = ⅞ : 3. Multiply both by 8 to clear the fraction:
A : B = 7 : 24
∴ the simplest formula is A₇B₂₄.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|21||0|0:
Freezing point depression is ΔTf = i·Kf·m, so the highest freezing point belongs to the
solution with the *smallest* ΔTf — the fewest particles. All are 0.1 molal, so only i matters.
Count the ions each formula unit gives:
(A) Al₂(SO₄)₃ ⇒ 2Al³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻, i = 5, effective 0.5
(C) AlCl₃ ⇒ Al³⁺ + 3Cl⁻, i = 4, effective 0.4
(B) BaCl₂ ⇒ Ba²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, i = 3, effective 0.3
(D) NH₄Cl ⇒ NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻, i = 2, effective 0.2 ← smallest
Fewest particles ⇒ least depression ⇒ the freezing point stays nearest to 0 °C.
∴ 0.1 molal NH₄Cl.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|22||0|0:
Colligative properties count particles, so they go wrong whenever the solute does not stay
as single formula units in solution.
The van't Hoff factor is the correction:
i = (observed colligative property) / (calculated value assuming no change)
  = (actual number of particles) / (number of formula units dissolved)
If the solute dissociates, particles increase and i > 1 — NaCl in water gives i ≈ 2.
If the solute associates, particles decrease and i < 1 — benzoic acid dimerises in benzene, i ≈ 0.5.
If neither happens, i = 1, as for urea or glucose.
So i measures how far the solute has broken up (or joined up), not how much of it dissolves.
∴ it accounts for the extent of dissociation of the solute.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|23||0|0.s:
In ordinary osmosis the solvent moves the other way: from the pure solvent, or the dilute side,
through the membrane *into* the more concentrated solution, driven by the difference in
chemical potential. The flow dilutes the solution.
Here the solvent is described as leaving the solution — the reverse of the natural direction.
That only happens if a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side.
The membrane passes solvent but holds back solute, so pure solvent is squeezed out and the
solution left behind becomes more concentrated.
This is reverse osmosis, and it is how sea water is desalinated.
(C) sorption and (D) dialysis are different processes entirely.
∴ reverse osmosis.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|24||0|0.s:
A reducing agent gives electrons away, so it is itself oxidised.
The easier a species is to oxidise, the more negative its standard *reduction* potential.
So rank by E° and take the lowest:
Zn²⁺/Zn  E° = −0.762 V ← lowest
H⁺/H₂   E° = 0.00 V
Cr³⁺/Cr  E° = +0.740 V (as printed here)
F₂/F⁻   E° = +2.87 V ← highest, so F₂ is the strongest *oxidising* agent, the opposite of what is asked
The most negative value belongs to zinc, so Zn metal loses electrons most readily:
Zn ⇒ Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
∴ Zn(s) is the strongest reducing agent.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|25||0|0.s:
This is Faraday's first law applied to the oxidation of chlorate to perchlorate.
Find the oxidation state change first:
In NaClO₃, Cl is +5. In NaClO₄, Cl is +7.
So each chlorine loses 2 electrons; forming 1 mol NaClO₄ needs 2 mol of electrons.
One faraday is one mole of electrons, so 3 F supplies 3 mol of electrons.
moles of NaClO₄ = (moles of electrons) / 2 = 3 / 2 = 1.5 mol
The H₂ appearing in the equation is the cathode product and does not affect this count.
∴ 1.5 mol of NaClO₄.
